revision_note_r5: Revised after plan_judge REJECT of plan@2c8bf8cc173d69d2a34d31efb90e0f21bc27dfe7. Every change is substantive; no qualifier was moved. (1) P-A0 had no declared boundary, so its manifest could not satisfy the Definition of Done. Fixed at the root: **T00 is now a real task** — declared in factory/.planning/decompose.json with a 14-path boundary, with factory/tasks/T00.md written, and T01..T05 now depend on it. The slice is renamed P-T00, its manifest is exactly T00's boundary, and the manifest now also carries factory/tasks/T05.md (omitted from the r4 claim), factory/BLUEPRINT.md, factory/.planning/plan.json, factory/HANDOFF.md and scripts/lib/check_amendments.py — the last three being the files the r4 rebuttal required but did not list. Its verification is no longer greps for isolated words: scripts/lib/check_amendments.py checks that each amended document carries its SUPERSEDED (C-N) marker, that the superseded text is inside a blockquote (no unquoted line may contain a stale token), and that a canonical sentence per conflict appears verbatim in every document that must agree, including plan.json and HANDOFF.md. (2) The --health exception is withdrawn, not reworded. The judge is right that neither an unavailable task goal nor a CI convention can create an exception to CONTRACT 0.2, and the CI premise is additionally false: .github/workflows/factory.yml and scripts/ were checked and neither invokes the CLI at all. 0.2 lists 'a missing argument' among the argv shapes that MUST be rejected, and `pomo --health` supplies no duration. So `pomo --health` is now a rejection, T02's positional goes back to being required (the nargs='?' complication and its silent-default trap disappear with it), and the documents that promised otherwise are amended by new conflict C-6. If the health check is wanted, that is a CONTRACT 0.2 amendment by the exam board before signature — recorded as an open item, not granted here. (3) P-T04's wrong final state for opposite signals pending together is fixed rather than declared residual. The transition record is no longer written by a Python handler in CPython's ascending-signal-number scan order: signal.set_wakeup_fd on an os.pipe() has CPython's C-level handler write the signal number at delivery, so the byte stream is in delivery order, and the render loop waits in select() on that pipe instead of sleeping. A resume delivered before a pause is now applied resume-then-pause and the interval ends paused. What survives is a few-instruction window inside trip_signal, stated honestly and no longer at a timescale any sender can observe. The handler now does nothing at all, so r4's under-warranted 'read the clock inside the handler' argument is gone with it. (4) P-T05 is redesigned, not rescoped. r4's short-write remainder loop broke 0.5's 'one append of the complete record' by construction; there is now exactly one os.write ever, and a short return is rolled back with ftruncate to the pre-write size so no torn line survives the call. Both preconditions the judge rejected are withdrawn: no local-filesystem scoping (the rollback covers a short return anywhere) and no conforming-pre-existing-log precondition (this program is the only writer the contract defines, so 'every line has four fields' is a property of what it writes). Directory durability is no longer an ambiguous singular parent: on the creating run every directory that gained an entry is fsynced — $HOME for .pomo/ and ~/.pomo for log.tsv. (5) P-T03's claim is scoped to the running state, since T04 stores a remaining duration while paused, and its verification now exercises SIGSTOP against a real process in tests/test_clock.py rather than leaving AC-5's stall half to a fake clock. (6) P-T02's verify now runs T01's tests/test_health.py, the regression it owns. (7) I-5 is new: visible/test_pause.py ends in assertWellFormed, so that module cannot pass before T05 lands; the verify commands say so instead of naming a gate that cannot go green.

disputed_review_notes.note: plan_judge r4 (P-T04): 'The admitted wrong final state when opposite signals are pending together is a contract failure, not an acceptable residual: 0.6 contains no spacing exception.'
disputed_review_notes.response: Accepted, and fixed rather than argued. Delivery order is recoverable — just not from the Python-level handlers, which CPython invokes in ascending signal-number order. signal.set_wakeup_fd(w) makes CPython's C-level handler write the signal number to a pipe at delivery, so the bytes are in delivery order; the loop waits in select() on the read end and applies each drained byte in the order it appears. Resume-then-pause now ends paused. One residual is left and it is smaller by orders of magnitude: the order inverts only if the second signal's delivery preempts the first inside the handful of instructions of trip_signal before its write. That is not a spacing exception at any timescale a sender can produce deliberately — it requires the two deliveries to overlap inside one C function — and it is a property of POSIX signal delivery rather than of an interval this implementation picked. It is stated, not claimed away.

disputed_review_notes.note: plan_judge r4 (P-T04): 'The accumulator rebuttal is also overstated — three SIGUSR1 deliveries do not establish duplicate resume application, and both representations already require the same state-change guard.'
disputed_review_notes.response: Accepted in full; the blast-radius rebuttal is deleted. Three pause signals say nothing about duplicate resume application, and the guard is common to both forms. What replaces it is the one difference that is structural rather than statistical: under `deadline = monotonic() + remaining` the pause *destroys* the deadline, so there is no state in which an interval keeps counting against a deadline set before it was paused. Under `deadline += now - paused_at` the old deadline survives the pause and correctness depends on an addition being performed later. AC-6's 'paused time is not deducted' is therefore unrepresentable in the first form and merely absent in the second. That is ADR-2's own argument, and it is adopted verbatim.

disputed_review_notes.note: plan_judge r4 (P-T05): 'Section 0.5 unconditionally requires one complete append and no crash-truncated line; the plan expressly disclaims both after a short write and then performs multiple writes.'
disputed_review_notes.response: Accepted in full. The remainder loop is removed. There is exactly one os.write() of the complete record on every path; a short return is rolled back with os.ftruncate() to the size captured before the write, and the program then reports the failure on stderr and exits non-zero without announcing a completion. So no path leaves a partial record and no path performs a second write. The only case in which the rollback is withheld is a short write that raced a second appender (the pre-write size no longer matches), because truncating there would destroy another process's record; that case is reported, not silently accepted, and its precondition is a full disk plus a concurrent pomo in the same instant.

disputed_review_notes.note: plan_judge r4 (P-T05): 'The local-filesystem and conforming-preexisting-log preconditions are also absent from the contract and therefore weaken it.'
disputed_review_notes.response: Accepted; both are withdrawn from the claim. The local-filesystem scoping was load-bearing only for the short-write case, which the rollback now handles on any filesystem. The conforming-log precondition was unnecessary: under this contract the program is the only writer of ~/.pomo/log.tsv (NG-4, NG-6, NG-7; B-02 is a reader), so 'every line has the same field count and the file ends with a newline' is a property of the records this program writes, and it writes exactly one shape. The operational rule that history is never read or repaired stays in the warrant, where it belongs, as a consequence of AC-8's scale budget.

disputed_review_notes.note: plan_judge r4 (P-T01/P-T02): '--health has no authority in the supplied contract and contradicts 0.2's valid-iff rule ... the plan cannot create an exception to 0.2 from an unavailable task goal or CI convention.'
disputed_review_notes.response: Accepted without reservation, and the check was run: `.github/workflows/factory.yml` and everything under `scripts/` were searched for an invocation of the CLI, and there is none — the workflow's build job runs `pip install -e . || true` and `bash -n`, nothing more. So the CI premise recorded in T01.md was false as well as insufficient. CONTRACT 0.2 lists 'a missing argument' among the shapes that MUST be rejected and `pomo --health` supplies no duration, so it is a rejection. C-6 amends T01.md, BLUEPRINT.md and (already applied) decompose.json's T01 goal; tests/test_health.py keeps its name and asserts the rejection plus entry-point resolution. Restoring the health check would require amending CONTRACT 0.2 before signature, which is the exam board's to do and is recorded as an open item under C-6.

authority_note: CONTRACT.md section 0 states that an implementation which disagrees with it fails, and the Definition of Done is the two suites passing with no file changed outside a task's declared boundary. Where an ADR, a task file, a blueprint line or a boundary disagrees with the contract, this plan follows the contract and the disagreement is fixed in the document that is wrong, before a builder reads it. Six conflicts were found; none is discretionary. C-1 (T01's boundary had no runnable entry point) was applied in revision 4. C-2..C-6 are document amendments, and revision 5 makes them a declared task rather than a floating work order: **T00** exists in factory/.planning/decompose.json with its own boundary and its own task file, and T01..T05 depend on it. That is what makes the fix legal under the Definition of Done — a builder's boundary is its permission, no builder's boundary contains an ADR or a task file, so a builder can neither follow an unamended document nor fix one, but T00's boundary does contain them. Nothing in this plan amends CONTRACT.md. Where the contract itself is the thing someone may want changed — the `--health` check under C-6 — that is recorded as an open item for the exam board and the human signature, not granted here.

contract_conflicts.contract: 0.1 — resolution order is $POMO_CMD, ./pomo, ./bin/pomo, ./pomo.py or ./src/pomo.py, then `pomo` on PATH; and 'Nothing else is required to run it: no install step.'
contract_conflicts.conflict: T01's boundary as decomposed (pyproject.toml, src/pomo/{__init__,__main__,cli,session}.py, tests/test_health.py) contained no path find_cmd() in factory/tests/visible/pomolib.py can resolve. run-visible.sh performs no install, so the pyproject console script only helps if `pip install -e .` has already run — which the contract explicitly says must not be required, and which the Definition of Done command does not do. Every visible and held-out test would fail in setUp with 'no pomo CLI found'.
contract_conflicts.resolution: The boundary was wrong and the boundary is what changed. `pomo` (an executable shim at the repo root, resolution slot 2) was added to the `Boundary:` line of factory/tasks/T01.md and to tasks[T01].boundary in factory/.planning/decompose.json in plan revision 4, together with a paragraph in T01.md stating why the shim exists, that it must be chmod +x, and that the pyproject console script stays as the pipx path for humans.
contract_conflicts.grants: APPLIED in revision 4 — factory/tasks/T01.md and factory/.planning/decompose.json. The two agree; neither may be re-narrowed without breaking CONTRACT 0.1. P-T01's manifest is inside its declared boundary.

contract_conflicts.contract: 0.6 — SIGUSR1 pauses, SIGUSR2 resumes, both idempotent, neither terminates.
contract_conflicts.conflict: ADR-2 and factory/tasks/T04.md specify `p`/`q` keypresses on stdin read via select(). That mechanism is not merely untested here, it is unreachable: pomolib.spawn() and examlib.spawn() both pass stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, so select() reports fd 0 readable-at-EOF on the first poll and ADR-2's own rule ('stdin closed or at EOF: stop polling it and run to completion') means no pause can ever occur. visible/test_pause.py and heldout/test_pause_semantics.py drive pause with proc.send_signal(signal.SIGUSR1), whose default disposition terminates the process.
contract_conflicts.resolution: Amend ADR-2 and T04.md with the canonical sentence 'SIGUSR1 pauses, SIGUSR2 resumes, both idempotent, neither terminates'. ADR-2's rejection of signals argued against a second command (needs a pid file and a daemon, NG-7, or a socket, AC-13) and against SIGTSTP (breaks Ctrl-Z, collides with AC-5's SIGSTOP); neither argument reaches SIGUSR1/2. ADR-2's time-accounting decision — store a duration, re-derive the deadline — is unaffected, is the load-bearing half of that ADR, and is adopted verbatim. Superseded text is blockquoted under a `SUPERSEDED (C-2)` marker, not deleted.
contract_conflicts.grants: T00 edits factory/adr/ADR-2.md and factory/tasks/T04.md. decompose.json's B-06 goal ('the p/q keys') was corrected to SIGUSR1/SIGUSR2 in revision 5. Knock-on: removing `q` removes the abandon path, which is where CONTRACT 0.7's non-zero-exit-on-interrupt used to live — see R-3 and I-3.

contract_conflicts.contract: 0.5 — field 1 is the interval completion time (datetime.fromisoformat-parseable); field 2 is the duration in whole minutes, equal to the CLI argument.
contract_conflicts.conflict: ADR-3 and factory/tasks/T05.md fix the order as started_at, ended_at, planned_minutes, ran_seconds. That puts the completion time in field 2 and the minutes in field 3. visible/test_log.py asserts line.split('\t')[1] == '1' directly, heldout/test_arg_boundaries.py asserts it equals '600', and both assertWellFormed helpers parse field 1 with datetime.fromisoformat.
contract_conflicts.resolution: Reorder to ended_at, planned_minutes, started_at, ran_seconds. All four ADR-3 columns survive, the field count stays fixed at 4, and ADR-3's 'every field is an integer or a timestamp so no field can contain a tab' argument for AC-10 is untouched — that argument is about the column *choice* and must not be blockquoted along with the column *order*.
contract_conflicts.grants: T00 edits the column table in factory/adr/ADR-3.md and in factory/tasks/T05.md.

contract_conflicts.contract: 0.4 — the countdown updates 'at least once per second of wall-clock time'; 0.3 — POMO_SECONDS_PER_MINUTE may be any positive decimal.
contract_conflicts.conflict: ADR-1 and factory/tasks/T03.md say the render loop sleeps to the next second boundary, `remaining % 1`. But `remaining` is in *nominal* units, and 0.3 places no bound on the scale factor at either end. Above 60 seconds-per-minute one nominal second is longer than one real second, so the loop refreshes less often than once per wall-clock second and violates 0.4/AC-3 while keeping perfect time. At an exact nominal boundary the remainder is zero, so the loop sleeps zero and can do so repeatedly. And at the held-out suite's smallest scale (0.005, used by `pomo 600`) a nominal second is 83 microseconds, so boundary-sleeping is a CPU-bound frame storm.
contract_conflicts.resolution: Amend ADR-1's render rule and T03.md's 'What to build' bullet to, all in real seconds: step_real = SECONDS_PER_MINUTE / 60; rem = remaining_real % step_real; tick = step_real if rem <= EPS else rem; sleep_for = max(min(tick, 1.0, remaining_real), MIN_SLEEP). ADR-1's decision — the deadline is monotonic and `remaining` is always derived, never decremented — is untouched and adopted verbatim; ADR-1 already states the sleep is a display concern with no effect on when the interval ends.
contract_conflicts.grants: T00 edits ADR-1's render rule and the matching bullet in factory/tasks/T03.md. Lower severity than C-1..C-3 and C-6 — it contradicts a subordinate rule inside ADR-1, not ADR-1's decision — but it is declared here rather than left inside a warrant.

contract_conflicts.contract: 0.2 — valid iff the argument is a single token matching ASCII ^[1-9][0-9]*$; everything else, including a missing argument and more than one argument, MUST be rejected.
contract_conflicts.conflict: factory/tasks/T02.md names a rejected set of five cases (`0`, `-5`, `2.5`, `abc`, missing) and repeats it as the 'Done when'. Read as the definition it appears to be, it is satisfied by `int(token) > 0`, which accepts `1_0`, `٣`, `５`, ` 5 `, and — via float — `1e1`, `inf` and `nan`, every one of which 0.2 rejects and heldout/test_arg_boundaries.py checks. T02.md also says nothing about argv shapes that are not durations at all, which is the cross-slice trap now that C-6 makes `pomo --health` a rejection: a parser change here can regress a T01 criterion T02 does not run.
contract_conflicts.resolution: Amend T02.md: validity is `re.fullmatch(r"[1-9][0-9]*", token)` on the **raw** token, the five cases are a sample of 0.2's rejected set rather than its definition, and 'the duration positional stays required, so a bare pomo and pomo --health both exit non-zero'. A required positional is what argparse gives for free: a missing duration and an unrecognized option are both non-zero with a stderr message, which is exactly 0.2's requirement. Revision 4's nargs='?' shape and its silent-default trap are withdrawn along with the --health exception (C-6).
contract_conflicts.grants: T00 edits factory/tasks/T02.md. No ADR is involved; no source file is touched.

contract_conflicts.contract: 0.2 — 'Valid iff the argument is a single token matching ASCII ^[1-9][0-9]*$. Everything else — ... a missing argument, more than one argument — is invalid and MUST be rejected per AC-2.'
contract_conflicts.conflict: T01's goal, factory/tasks/T01.md and factory/BLUEPRINT.md (task table, the 'why T01 is the skeleton' paragraph, and the decompose-gate checklist line) all require `pomo --health` to print ok and exit 0. `pomo --health` supplies no duration, and 0.2 names a missing argument among the shapes that MUST be rejected — so there is no reading of 0.2 under which that exit status is legal. The justification T01.md records for the exception is 'CI calls it'; .github/workflows/factory.yml and scripts/ were checked and neither invokes the CLI at all, so the exception has no authority and no user either. Revisions 3 and 4 tried to carry it as a stated exception; that was the plan granting itself an amendment to a contract it does not own.
contract_conflicts.resolution: The contract wins and the health check goes. Canonical sentence for every document: 'pomo --health is rejected with a non-zero exit, like any other argv that does not supply a valid duration'. tests/test_health.py keeps its name and its place in T01's boundary and is repurposed — the entry point resolves from a clean checkout with no install step, `./pomo --health` exits non-zero with a message on stderr and no countdown, and a short scaled interval exits 0. BLUEPRINT's checklist item is replaced by the property the health check was a proxy for: T01's entry point resolves per 0.1 with no install step. OPEN ITEM for the exam board and the human signature: if a health check is wanted, it needs an amendment to CONTRACT 0.2 carving out non-duration argv, made before the contract is signed. This plan does not grant it and no slice implements it.
contract_conflicts.grants: APPLIED in revision 5 for decompose.json (tasks[T01].goal no longer mentions the health check). T00 edits factory/tasks/T01.md and factory/BLUEPRINT.md.

contract_requirements_no_task_owns.contract: 0.3 — POMO_SECONDS_PER_MINUTE, a positive decimal giving the wall-clock seconds in one nominal minute. Default 60 when unset **or empty**. Scales real interval length only; must not change the displayed remaining time, the logged duration, or argument validation.
contract_requirements_no_task_owns.gap: No task file, ADR, or BLUEPRINT line mentions it. Without it the shortest observable interval is 60s and AC-3/5/6/7 are untestable; every visible and held-out test spawns with it set, as `repr(float(scale))` — so the parser must accept plain decimal forms like '1.0', '6.0', '0.5' and '0.005'.
contract_requirements_no_task_owns.assigned: P-T01 reads it in session.py (in boundary). P-T03 moves it into clock.py as the nominal-to-real scale factor (in boundary). No boundary amendment needed. Both slices pin: unset or empty string means 60.0; the value is parsed once with float() at startup; a non-positive or unparseable value is a startup error, not a silent fallback.

contract_requirements_no_task_owns.contract: 0.4 — countdown goes to stdout even when stdout is a pipe, flushed immediately, rendered as zero-padded MM:SS in *nominal* units, at least once per second of **wall-clock** time.
contract_requirements_no_task_owns.gap: T01.md says 'render a countdown' without pinning the flush, the nominal-units rule, or the real-second cadence. A block-buffered stream that only appears at exit fails AC-3 while keeping perfect time.
contract_requirements_no_task_owns.assigned: P-T01 (flush, nominal units, real-second cadence); P-T03 restates the cadence rule once a scale factor exists, with the zero-remainder and minimum-sleep cases (C-4); P-T04 keeps it while paused by re-emitting the frozen frame at the same 1.0s upper bound.

contract_requirements_no_task_owns.contract: 0.7 — non-zero exit on interrupt before completion; AC-12 — an interrupted interval appends no line.
contract_requirements_no_task_owns.gap: Under ADR-2 this was carried by the `q` abandon path. C-2 removes `q`, so no slice owned it any more. There is no other 'abandon' concept in the contract: 0.6's two signals are the only ones the program handles deliberately. heldout/test_crash.py checks it for SIGKILL, SIGINT and SIGTERM alike.
contract_requirements_no_task_owns.assigned: P-T05, which owns AC-12. The rule is: do not replace the disposition of SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP or SIGQUIT. Stated precisely, because the two halves differ. SIGTERM/SIGHUP/SIGQUIT have no Python handler, so the OS default terminates the process with a non-zero wait status. SIGINT does have one — CPython installs default_int_handler at startup — and it raises KeyboardInterrupt, which left uncaught exits 1 with a traceback on stderr. Both are non-zero, and neither appends anything, because the write sits after the interval reaches zero and not in a finally. The deliberate non-action is therefore: no signal.signal() call for these four, and no `except KeyboardInterrupt` that exits 0. A friendly abandon message is backlog B-04 and must keep the non-zero exit.

contract_requirements_no_task_owns.contract: 0.5 — the log path is '$HOME/.pomo/log.tsv, resolved from the environment at run time'.
contract_requirements_no_task_owns.gap: No task file says 'at run time'. A module-level `os.path.expanduser('~')` evaluated at import, or a cached constant, is the natural thing to write and is wrong under both harnesses, which set HOME per spawned process — and examlib.fresh_home() changes it again mid-test.
contract_requirements_no_task_owns.assigned: P-T05 — the path is computed inside the write function from os.environ at the moment of the append.

integration_notes.note: T03, T04 and T05 each rewrite part of session.py in sequence, and a slice's `verify` runs only the visible modules that can pass at that point plus the unit test its own boundary adds. Ownership: the builder runs its slice's verify; the **inspector** owns the Definition of Done — `bash factory/tests/run-visible.sh` twice in a row plus `run-heldout.sh` — and that gate cannot be delegated to a builder, because no builder worktree contains factory/tests/heldout/. This is why the DoD asks for the full suite rather than an aggregate of the five verify commands.

T02 sits outside the T01→T03→T04→T05 spine and touches only cli.py, so it can land at any point after T00 and T01. Its boundary is disjoint from every other build task, so there is no merge hazard — but it is the only slice whose verify exercises the reject path, and after C-6 it is also the slice that can regress T01's argv behaviour without owning it. That is why P-T02's verify runs tests/test_health.py. Later slices must not move validation out of cli.py to reach it.

C-2 deletes the `q` abandon path that T04.md and ADR-2 describe. T05.md's 'not on T04's q path' instruction becomes vacuous — the equivalent rule is 'the write is not in a finally and not reachable from any signal path'. R-3 carries the exit-code half, and states the SIGINT case precisely because CPython does not leave SIGINT at its OS default.

T00 is a prerequisite of all five build tasks, including T01 — C-6 amends T01.md and BLUEPRINT.md, so T01 is no longer independent of the amendments. The ordering is not bureaucratic: T03.md, T04.md and T05.md each open with 'read factory/adr/ADR-N.md before writing code', so an unamended ADR is the first thing the builder reads and plan.json is the second, if at all. T00 changes no file under src/, tests/ or factory/tests/, so it cannot move either suite; its only failure mode is leaving two documents disagreeing, which is exactly what its verify checks.

The visible suite is not fully green until T05 lands, and no slice's verify pretends otherwise. visible/test_log.py needs T05 by definition. Less obviously, visible/test_pause.py's AC-6 test ends with `self.assertWellFormed(self.read_log_bytes(), expect_lines=1)` — so the pause module cannot pass at T04, whose boundary contains no log writer. P-T04 therefore verifies against test_run plus its own tests/test_pause.py, and P-T05's verify is the first gate that runs `run-visible.sh test_pause`. HANDOFF.md's 'run the whole suite before you finish' is corrected to match: modules owned by tasks that have not landed yet will fail, and that is not your slice's failure — every criterion an earlier slice established still is.

T04 changes how the render loop waits, not how long. T03 pins the duration (the C-4 formula); T04 replaces `time.sleep(sleep_for)` with `select.select([wakeup_r], [], [], sleep_for)` so that a signal wakes the loop immediately instead of at the end of the current sleep. The formula, the units, and the deadline are T03's and stay untouched — a T04 that reintroduces its own polling interval is re-solving a problem select() already solved and reintroduces the accounting error I-1's ordering exists to avoid.

slices.claim: Before any builder picks up T01, T02, T03, T04 or T05, the five document amendments C-2, C-3, C-4, C-5 and C-6 are applied to factory/adr/ADR-1.md, factory/adr/ADR-2.md, factory/adr/ADR-3.md, factory/tasks/T01.md, factory/tasks/T02.md, factory/tasks/T03.md, factory/tasks/T04.md, factory/tasks/T05.md and factory/BLUEPRINT.md — each amendment keeping the superseded text verbatim inside a blockquote under a `SUPERSEDED (C-N)` marker that names the contract section which overrode it, and each stating its replacement in a canonical sentence repeated verbatim in every document that must agree, including factory/.planning/plan.json and factory/HANDOFF.md — so that every document a builder is told to read agrees with CONTRACT section 0, no ADR or task file appears in any builder's file manifest, and scripts/lib/check_amendments.py exits 0. factory/tasks/T00.md is in the manifest because a task's own file is where its later amendments belong; factory/.planning/decompose.json is in it because that is where T00 and the T01..T05 dependency edges live.

slices.warrant: Three facts force this into a task of its own, and revision 5 gives it the one thing it was missing — a boundary. First, the Definition of Done says no file outside a task's declared boundary changed. No builder boundary contains an ADR or a task document, so a builder who notices a conflict and fixes the ADR fails the DoD, and a builder who obeys the ADR fails the contract. There is no third option available to a builder. The r4 plan drew the right conclusion and then left the work in a slice with no declared boundary, which fails the same rule it was invoking; declaring T00 in decompose.json with its own boundary and its own task file is what actually closes it, and it is the same move C-1 made for T01. Second, the reading order makes the unamended document win by default: T03.md, T04.md and T05.md each open with 'Read factory/adr/ADR-N.md before writing code', HANDOFF tells the builder to read its task file first, and plan.json is a document the builder may never open. An amendment applied after the builder has started is an amendment that arrived too late — which is why T01..T05 now depend on T00 rather than merely being advised to wait. Third, these edits are inert with respect to both suites: nothing under src/, tests/ or factory/tests/ is touched, so the usual reason to fold a change into the slice that needs it does not apply, and the usual reason not to does. The amendments are amendments, not rewrites, and the format is mechanical so that it can be checked: superseded text stays verbatim in a blockquote under a `SUPERSEDED (C-N)` marker naming the overriding section, and the replacement is stated outside it in a canonical sentence. That format is what makes verification possible, and verification is where r4 was weakest — greps for the word 'health' or 'real' prove nothing about whether the old rule is still standing three paragraphs down. scripts/lib/check_amendments.py checks the three properties that matter: (a) every canonical sentence appears verbatim in each document that must agree, including plan.json and HANDOFF.md, so 'the documents agree' is a string identity rather than a judgement; (b) every amended file carries its SUPERSEDED marker; (c) no *unquoted* line in the nine amended documents contains a stale token — `cbreak` or `keypress` for C-2, ``1 | `started_at` `` for C-3, `remaining % 1` for C-4, `prints ok` or ``prints `ok` `` for C-6 — so old text that was left standing outside a blockquote is a failure rather than an oversight. The script is a transcription of the `contract_conflicts` table in this file, listed there token by token so a reviewer can diff the two. What must not be lost in the editing is the reasoning that was right: ADR-2's argument against a second command and against SIGTSTP still holds, and ADR-3's 'every field is an integer or a timestamp, so no field can contain a tab' is the load-bearing argument for AC-10 — deleting the surrounding text to fix the column order would destroy the reasoning that makes the column order safe.
rebuttal: The amendments are skipped on the grounds that plan.json already records them. The builder reads its task file and the ADR first — both still say `p`/`q`, `started_at` first, `remaining % 1`, and `--health` prints ok — so the unamended document is what gets implemented, and four slices fail on instructions the plan believed it had corrected.

A builder applies an amendment itself when it hits the conflict. The change lands in factory/adr/ or factory/tasks/, outside that builder's boundary, and the Definition of Done fails on the boundary check even though every test passes. T00's boundary is the only boundary those paths are inside.

T00 is declared but T01..T05's `depends` edges are dropped as noise, so the foreman schedules T01 first. T01 is the one task that used to be independent of the amendments and no longer is: C-6 changes its goal, its task file, and what tests/test_health.py asserts.

The ADRs are rewritten rather than amended. ADR-2's reasoning against a second command and ADR-3's tab-freedom argument disappear with the text that was wrong, and the next person to touch pause or the log format re-derives — or fails to re-derive — an argument that had already been made.

The old rule is left standing outside the blockquote while the new one is added below it, so both are present and the builder implements whichever it read first. This is the failure the unquoted-stale-token check exists to catch, and it is the most likely one: it looks like a completed amendment in a diff.

check_amendments.py is written to pass rather than to check — it greps for a word that appears in both the old and the new text, or omits the unquoted-line rule. The canonical sentences and stale tokens are enumerated in this file precisely so that the script can be diffed against the plan rather than trusted.
The amendment lands after a builder has already created its worktree. The worktree carries the old T04.md, and the amendment is invisible to the process that needed it.

The canonical sentences are paraphrased into each document instead of copied. Every paraphrase is a document that disagrees by string identity, the check fails, and the reviewer cannot tell a wording preference from a substantive divergence — which is the whole reason the check is a string comparison.

T00's edits land but plan.json and HANDOFF.md are not re-synced, so three documents disagree about which resolution is current. Both files are in the manifest and in the boundary, and both are checked for every canonical sentence, so this fails loudly instead of silently.

C-6 is read as licence to delete the health check from the source as well. There is no source yet — that is the point — but a later reader could take the amendment as authority over CONTRACT 0.2 itself. The amendment says the opposite: restoring `--health` is an exam-board contract change before signature.

slices.claim: `./pomo N` resolves from a clean checkout with no install step, blocks for the whole nominal interval, streams a zero-padded MM:SS countdown to stdout at least once per real second even when stdout is a pipe, then prints a completion summary naming the finished interval and telling the user in plain text to take a break, and exits 0 leaving no process alive in its process group; POMO_SECONDS_PER_MINUTE (default 60 when unset or empty) scales the real duration only, never the displayed remaining time; and an argv that does not supply a single valid duration token — `./pomo --health` included — exits non-zero with a message on stderr, renders no countdown and creates no ~/.pomo. T02 owns the full rejected set of CONTRACT 0.2; what this slice claims is that the shape of the parser here does not have to be undone to get there.

grounds.depends_on_amendment: C-6 (T00) — T01.md and BLUEPRINT.md require `pomo --health` to print ok and exit 0, which CONTRACT 0.2 forbids.
grounds.boundary_amendment: None outstanding. `pomo` was added to T01's boundary in factory/tasks/T01.md and factory/.planning/decompose.json in revision 4 (C-1, applied). tests/test_health.py keeps its name and its place in the boundary; C-6 changes what it asserts, not where it lives. Every path in this manifest is inside the declared boundary.
grounds.verify: bash factory/tests/run-visible.sh test_run && python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t . -p 'test_health.py'

slices.warrant: The contract resolves ./pomo (slot 2) before it ever consults PATH (slot 5) and states outright that no install step may be required; run-visible.sh runs no install. So a pyproject console script alone leaves find_cmd() returning None and all four visible modules failing in setUp before a line of timer code is exercised. A five-line executable ./pomo that prepends src/ to sys.path and calls cli.main() makes resolution work from a bare checkout, costs nothing, and leaves the console script in place for humans installing with pipx. That path is inside the boundary rather than requested from outside it, because a boundary that makes its own task's tests unrunnable is the artefact that is wrong. The health check goes the other way, and for the same reason in reverse: 0.2 says a duration is valid *iff* it matches the regex and names 'a missing argument' among the shapes that MUST be rejected, so `pomo --health` — which supplies no duration — is a rejection, and no task goal, blueprint line or CI convention can carve an exception out of a contract this plan does not own. The CI premise was checked and is false: nothing in .github/workflows/factory.yml or scripts/ invokes the CLI. C-6 amends the documents; tests/test_health.py is repurposed to assert the rejection and the entry-point resolution, which is the property the health check was really standing in for. Nothing else about T01 changes, because with no --health flag the parser is one required positional and argparse's own error path supplies the non-zero exit and the stderr message. AC-3 has two independent halves and each is satisfied by construction rather than by tuning. Cadence: the loop's wait is bounded above by one real second and below by a small floor, measured in real seconds, so at least one frame is emitted per wall-clock second at every scale — 0.3 puts no ceiling on POMO_SECONDS_PER_MINUTE, so a rule expressed purely in nominal units cannot establish a wall-clock guarantee, and the exact formula (with its zero-remainder and floor cases) is pinned by P-T03 once a scale factor has a home. Delivery: each frame is written as MM:SS *followed by* `\r`, with flush=True. The order matters and is pinned because 0.4 says each update is 'terminated by \r or \n' — a leading `\r` prefixes the next frame instead of ending the current one, which leaves the final frame unterminated and makes the stream's frame boundaries depend on the next write ever happening. Flushing removes the only other realistic failure mode for a piped countdown: Python block-buffers a non-TTY stdout, so an unflushed but perfectly-timed countdown arrives in one lump at exit and fails a test the implementer will read as a timing bug. The MM:SS value is derived from the *nominal* remaining time, never from the scaled real time, because 0.3 says the hook must not change what is displayed; concretely, `pomo 1` renders 01:00 down to 00:00 whether the scale is 1.0 or 60. The scale itself is parsed once at startup with float() from os.environ, treating unset and empty alike as 60.0 and treating a non-positive or unparseable value as a startup error, because 0.3 specifies a default for absence but not a fallback for garbage and a silent fallback would hide a mis-set harness. AC-13 needs no code at all: a single-threaded foreground loop that spawns nothing, binds nothing, and starts no non-daemon thread has nothing that could outlive main — which is why it is cheap to honour now and expensive to retrofit after T04 adds signal state. Per T01.md the end time is computed once up front and the loop runs until the clock passes it; `remaining -= 1` is not written here, so T03 hardens this shape instead of undoing it.
rebuttal: The C-1 boundary correction is reverted, or ./pomo is dropped as 'not in the original decomposition'. Then no in-boundary path satisfies CONTRACT 0.1 without an install step, find_cmd() returns None, and every module in both suites fails in setUp with 'no pomo CLI found' regardless of how correct the timer is.

./pomo is created without the executable bit. find_cmd() checks os.access(p, os.X_OK) and silently skips it, falling through to slot 5 — so the suite passes only on a machine where `pip install -e .` happened to have run: green locally, red on a clean checkout.
./pomo imports the package by name without putting src/ on sys.path, so it works only from an installed environment — the same failure as the console script, moved one file over.

C-6 is not applied and `--health` is implemented as a flag that exits 0. No test in either suite catches it, which is exactly the danger: the repo ships an argv shape CONTRACT 0.2 says MUST be rejected, and the contract is what a signature makes immutable.

C-6 is applied but read as licence to drop tests/test_health.py. The file is in T01's boundary and is the only check that the entry point resolves without an install step — the failure mode C-1 exists to prevent has no other test.

The countdown is printed without flush=True. stdout is a pipe under test, so the whole countdown arrives at exit: test_ac3 sees one arrival instead of five and reports a cadence failure for a buffering bug.

Frames are written `\r`-prefixed rather than `\r`-terminated. 0.4 requires each update to be terminated; a leading carriage return leaves the last frame unterminated and makes each frame's boundary depend on the next write happening at all.

The wait is a flat nominal second. At POMO_SECONDS_PER_MINUTE above 60 the countdown refreshes slower than once per wall-clock second and AC-3 fails with the timing perfect. The visible suite only spawns at scales 1.0 and 6.0, both below 60, so this passes locally and is caught only by the held-out suite — or by nobody.

POMO_SECONDS_PER_MINUTE is applied to the displayed remaining time as well as to the real duration. `pomo 1` at scale 6 then renders 00:06 down to 00:00 instead of 01:00, violating 0.4 and yielding too few distinct MM:SS values for test_ac3's four-distinct-frames assertion.
An empty POMO_SECONDS_PER_MINUTE is passed to float() and raises, or is treated as 0 and divides by zero, instead of falling back to 60. 0.3 names unset and empty together.

The completion summary omits the duration. test_ac4 requires the digits of the requested minutes to appear in the last six frames, so 'Done! Take a break.' alone fails a criterion the implementer will believe is met.
The countdown is rendered with a background thread to decouple display from timing. AC-13 then depends on the thread being a daemon and on it actually exiting, rather than on there being no thread.
